claim: Passive translational diffusion typically limits the rates with which cytoplasmic proteins can reach their locations inside prokaryotic cells.
source: Inside prokaryotic cells, passive translational diffusion typically limits the rates with which cytoplasmic proteins can reach their locations.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a general principle about prokaryotic cells.

claim: The concentration of macromolecules in the bacterial cytoplasm is around 300 mg/ml for Escherichia coli.
source: For Escherichia coli, it is around 300 mg/ml, which corresponds to a volume fraction of 25–30% (Cayley et al., 1991; Zimmerman and Trach, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cayley et al., 1991 and Zimmerman and Trach, 1991.

claim: The concentration of macromolecules in E. coli cytoplasm corresponds to a volume fraction of 25–30%.
source: For Escherichia coli, it is around 300 mg/ml, which corresponds to a volume fraction of 25–30% (Cayley et al., 1991; Zimmerman and Trach, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cayley et al., 1991 and Zimmerman and Trach, 1991.

claim: Diffusion of free GFP is 3–4 times slower in the eukaryotic cytoplasm compared to water.
source: Compared to water, the diffusion of a free green fluorescent protein (GFP) was reported to be 3–4 times slower in the eukaryotic cytoplasm (Swaminathan et al., 1997)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Swaminathan et al., 1997.

claim: Diffusion of free GFP is up to 10 times slower in the bacterial cytoplasm compared to water.
source: and up to 10 times slower in the bacterial cytoplasm (Elowitz et al., 1999; Nenninger et al., 2010; Mika et al., 2010; Kumar et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The exponent β for the relationship between hydrodynamic radius R and molecular mass MM is within the range of 0.35–0.43 for typical proteins.
source: where the exponent β would be 1/3 for perfectly compact and globular proteins but is in practice within the range of 0.35–0.43 for typical proteins, reflecting the fractal nature of the spatial distribution of protein mass (Smilgies and Folta-Stogniew, 2015; Enright and Leitner, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Smilgies and Folta-Stogniew, 2015 and Enright and Leitner, 2005.

claim: Several studies of protein diffusion in E. coli cytoplasm have yielded different dependencies on molecular mass, from ~0.33 to ~2.
source: Several studies of protein diffusion in the cytoplasm of E. coli have yielded different dependencies on the molecular mass, from ~0.33 (Nenninger et al., 2010) to ~2 (Kumar et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nenninger et al., 2010 and Kumar et al., 2010.

claim: An average β of ~0.7 was estimated for protein diffusion in E. coli based on data pooled from multiple studies.
source: with an average β~0.7 estimated based on the data pooled from multiple studies (Mika and Poolman, 2011; Kalwarczyk et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mika and Poolman, 2011 and Kalwarczyk et al., 2012.

claim: An exponent of ~0.7 was observed for limited sets of differently sized proteins in E. coli.
source: Similar exponent of ~0.7 was observed for limited sets of differently sized proteins (Mika et al., 2010; Stracy et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mika et al., 2010 and Stracy et al., 2021.

claim: Early FRAP studies provided values of diffusion coefficient for GFP in E. coli ranging from 3 to 14 µm2 s–1.
source: These measurements provided values of diffusion coefficient for GFP ranging from 3 to 14 µm2 s–1 (Elowitz et al., 1999; Mullineaux et al., 2006; Konopka et al., 2009; Kumar et al., 2010; Mika et al., 2010; Nenninger et al., 2010; Schavemaker et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple FRAP studies.

claim: SPT and FCS measurements provided values of DGFP from 8 µm2 s–1 up to 18 µm2 s–1 in E. coli.
source: Both methods provided higher but still varying values of DGFP, from 8 µm2 s–1 up to 18 µm2 s–1 (Meacci et al., 2006; English et al., 2011; Sanamrad et al., 2014; Diepold et al., 2017; Rocha et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple SPT and FCS studies.

claim: A library of 31 cytoplasmic proteins of E. coli fused to sfGFP was generated for the analysis of cytoplasmic protein mobility.
source: For our analysis of cytoplasmic protein mobility, we generated a plasmid-encoded library of 31 cytoplasmic proteins (Table 1) of E. coli fused to superfolder GFP (sfGFP) (Pédelacq et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Table 1.

claim: ThpR-sfGFP showed >20% degradation to free sfGFP and was excluded from further analyses.
source: Only one of the constructs, ThpR-sfGFP, showed >20% degradation to free sfGFP, and it was therefore excluded from further analyses.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: All remaining constructs have pI ranging from 5.1 to 6.2, as common for cytoplasmic proteins.
source: This was also the sole construct with an atypically high isoelectric point (pI), and all remaining constructs have pI ranging from 5.1 to 6.2, as common for cytoplasmic proteins (Schwartz et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schwartz et al., 2001.

claim: RihA-sfGFP and NagD-sfGFP were excluded from the study due to non-uniform localization.
source: Except for RihA-sfGFP and NagD-sfGFP that were subsequently excluded, all other constructs showed uniform localization (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 1A.

claim: Expression of most fusion proteins used for diffusion measurements had little effect on E. coli growth.
source: Expression of most fusion proteins used for the measurements of diffusion had little effect on E. coli growth (Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cell length was moderately (approximately twofold) increased by treatment with cephalexin for 45 min, yielding an average cell length of ~5 μm.
source: In order to reduce the impact of photobleaching on FCS measurements, cell length was moderately (approximately twofold) increased by treatment with the cell-division inhibitor cephalexin for 45 min, yielding an average cell length of ~5 μm (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 1A.

claim: The anomalous diffusion model proved to be considerably better in fitting the experimental FCS data than the Brownian diffusion model.
source: Although we initially considered both the Brownian diffusion and the anomalous diffusion models, the latter model proved to be considerably better in fitting the experimental data (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: No significant correlation was observed between the values of 1/τD or α and the length or the width of individual cells.
source: As another control, we observed no significant correlation between the values of 1/τD or α and the length or the width of individual cells, although a weak trend of α increasing with cell width might exist (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 7.

claim: No significant effect of cephalexin treatment on the value of α was observed when individual cephalexin-treated and untreated cells of similar length were compared.
source: Finally, when individual cephalexin-treated and untreated cells of similar length were compared, we observed no effect of the treatment on the value of α and only marginal (p=0.08) increase in the mobility of sfGFP (Figure 1—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 8.

claim: The mean values of the diffusion time were clearly different between protein constructs.
source: Despite their substantial intercellular variability, the obtained mean values of the diffusion time were clearly different between protein constructs (Figure 1C and Table 1).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 1C and Table 1.

claim: Mobility of more than half of the constructs decreased uniformly with their molecular mass.
source: This dependence revealed a clear trend, where mobility of more than half of the constructs decreased uniformly with their molecular mass, while some exhibited much lower mobility than the other constructs of similar mass.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 1D.

claim: The anomalous diffusion exponent α showed no apparent dependence on the protein size, ranging from 0.8 to 0.86 for most of the constructs.
source: In contrast, the anomalous diffusion exponent α showed no apparent dependence on the protein size, ranging from 0.8 to 0.86 for most of the constructs (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 1E.

claim: The few protein constructs with α of ~0.8 or lower were also among the ones with low mobility for their molecular mass.
source: Notably, the few protein constructs with α of ~0.8 or lower were also among the ones with low mobility for their molecular mass (Figure 1D and E, colored symbols).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 1D and E.

claim: ClpS is the adaptor protein that delivers degradation substrates to the protease ClpAP.
source: ClpS is the adaptor protein that delivers degradation substrates to the protease ClpAP (Román-Hernández et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Román-Hernández et al., 2011.

claim: The substrate-binding site of ClpS is constituted by three amino acid residues (D35, D36, and H66).
source: The substrate-binding site of ClpS is constituted by three amino acid residues (D35, D36, and H66) that interact with the N-terminal degron of target proteins (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Román-Hernández et al., 2011 and Figure 1F.

claim: Mutation of D35, D36, and H66 to alanine substantially reduces substrate binding of ClpS in vitro.
source: If these residues are mutated into alanine, substrate binding in vitro is substantially reduced (Román-Hernández et al., 2011; Humbard et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Román-Hernández et al., 2011 and Humbard et al., 2013.

claim: The mobility of ClpSD35A_D36A_H66A-sfGFP in a ΔclpA strain became significantly higher and less anomalous, with both 1/τD and α reaching levels similar to those of other proteins of similar mass.
source: Consistently, we observed that while the stability of the mutant construct ClpSD35A_D36A_H66A-sfGFP was not affected (Figure 1—figure supplement 9), its mobility in a ΔclpA strain became significantly higher and less anomalous, with both 1/τD and α reaching levels similar to those of other proteins of similar mass (Figure 1D and E and Figure 1—figure supplement 10).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 1D, E, and Figure 1—figure supplement 9 and 10.

claim: Map is the methionine aminopeptidase that cleaves the N-terminal methionine from nascent polypeptide chains.
source: Map is the methionine aminopeptidase that cleaves the N-terminal methionine from nascent polypeptide chains (Solbiati et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Solbiati et al., 1999.

claim: Map interacts with the negatively charged backbone of ribosomes through four positively charged lysine residues (K211, 218, 224, and 226).
source: Map interacts with the negatively charged backbone of ribosomes through four positively charged lysine residues (K211, 218, 224, and 226) located in a loop (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sandikci et al., 2013 and Figure 1G.

claim: Mutation of K211, 218, 224, and 226 to alanine reduces the in vitro affinity of Map for the ribosomes.
source: If these residues are mutated into alanine, the in vitro affinity of Map for the ribosomes is reduced (Sandikci et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sandikci et al., 2013.

claim: The mobility of Map-sfGFP was much increased by alanine substitutions at all four lysine sites.
source: The mobility of Map-sfGFP was indeed much increased by alanine substitutions at all four lysine sites (Figure 1D and E and Figure 1—figure supplement 9 and Figure 1—figure supplement 10).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 1D, E, and Figure 1—figure supplement 9 and 10.

claim: DnaK is the major bacterial chaperone that binds to short hydrophobic polypeptide sequences.
source: DnaK is the major bacterial chaperone that binds to short hydrophobic polypeptide sequences, which become exposed during protein synthesis, membrane translocation, or protein unfolding (Genevaux et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Genevaux et al., 2007.

claim: The substitution of valine 436 with phenylalanine in DnaK markedly decreases substrate binding in vitro.
source: The substitution of the valine residue 436 with bulkier phenylalanine creates steric hindrance that markedly decreases substrate binding to DnaK in vitro (Mayer et al., 2000)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mayer et al., 2000.

claim: Both the 1/τD and α of DnaKV436F-sfGFP were significantly higher than for the correspondent wild-type construct.
source: and both the 1/τD and α of DnaKV436F-sfGFP were significantly higher than for the correspondent wild-type construct (Figure 1D and E and Figure 1—figure supplement 9 and Figure 1—figure supplement 10).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 1D, E, and Figure 1—figure supplement 9 and 10.

claim: For cell diameters of 0.8–0.9 μm and over a wide range of particle diffusion coefficients, simulated ACFs could be successfully fitted with the anomalous diffusion model, yielding an anomalous diffusion exponent of around 0.8–0.9.
source: For the values of cell diameter commonly observed under our growth conditions, 0.8–0.9 μm, and over a wide range of particle diffusion coefficients, simulated ACFs could be indeed successfully fitted with the anomalous diffusion model, yielding an anomalous diffusion exponent of around 0.8–0.9 (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 2A and B.

claim: The range of fit values of α observed for experimental data, 0.82–0.9, corresponded to the ansatz values of 0.95–1.0 in simulations of fractional Brownian motion under confinement.
source: The range of fit values observed for experimental data, 0.82–0.9, corresponded to the ansatz values of 0.95–1.0, hence very close to Brownian diffusion.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Treatment with A22 increased E. coli cell width.
source: In apparent agreement with these simulation results, when E. coli cell width was increased by treatment with the inhibitor of bacterial cell wall biosynthesis A22 (Ouzounov et al., 2016; Figure 2C)
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 2C.

claim: Treatment with A22 significantly increased the anomalous diffusion exponent of sfGFP.
source: the anomalous diffusion exponent of sfGFP (Figure 2D) also significantly increased.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 2D.

claim: Treatment with cephalexin slightly decreased the density of E. coli cells by 1 g/L.
source: The treatment with cephalexin slightly, by 1 g/L, that is <0.1% of E. coli volumetric mass density 1.11 kg/L (Martínez-Salas et al., 1981), decreased the density of E. coli cells in this assay.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The additional treatment with A22 had only minor and not significant impact on cell density once the effect of the A22-induced cell volume increase on sedimentation was accounted for.
source: The additional treatment with A22, in our growth conditions, had only minor and not significant impact, once the effect of the A22-induced cell volume increase on sedimentation was accounted for (Figure 2—figure supplement 3H–J).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 3H–J.

claim: FCS measurements with a smaller confocal volume (pinhole size 0.66 Airy units) yielded significantly higher values of α (>0.9) for sfGFP and AcnA-sfGFP.
source: Consistent with our expectation, the value of α derived from these measurements was significantly higher, >0.9, for sfGFP and AcnA-sfGFP (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claim: The anomalous diffusion exponent of DnaK-sfGFP remained low even when measured away from the cell boundary, confirming that its motion is truly subdiffusive due to interactions with other proteins.
source: In contrast, the anomalous diffusion exponent of DnaK-sfGFP remained low even when measured away from the cell boundary, confirming that its motion is truly subdiffusive due to interactions with other proteins.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claim: The OU model directly estimates the ansatz diffusion coefficient with ±5% accuracy for the typical cell widths observed in the experiments.
source: The OU model directly estimates the ansatz diffusion coefficient with ±5% accuracy for the typical cell widths observed in our experiments (Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claim: The dependence of D on molecular mass for the set of faster-diffusing constructs was scaling as (MM)−β with β=0.56±0.05.
source: The dependence of D on molecular mass for this set of constructs was scaling as (MM)−β with β=0.56±0.05 (Figure 2F, solid blue line)
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 2F.

claim: The diffusion coefficients determined by FRAP were 5–30% lower than those obtained from the FCS data for most constructs.
source: We observed very good correlation between both values of diffusion coefficients, although for most constructs the diffusion coefficients determined by FRAP were 5–30% lower than those obtained from the FCS data (Figure 3C and Table 1).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 3C and Table 1.

claim: All constructs of non-native proteins showed slight but mostly significantly increased anomaly of diffusion compared to E. coli proteins.
source: In contrast, all constructs showed slight but mostly significantly increased anomaly of diffusion compared to E. coli proteins (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Higher ionic strength significantly decreased the mobility of sfGFP.
source: Higher ionic strength also significantly decreased the mobility of sfGFP (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The mobility of all tested constructs decreased proportionally upon osmotic upshift.
source: Importantly, the mobility of all other tested constructs decreased proportionally (Figure 5A)
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 5A.

claim: No effect of osmotic upshift was observed on the anomaly of diffusion for any protein construct.
source: No effect was observed on the anomaly of diffusion for any protein construct (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The measured increase in mobility of sfGFP and two other constructs by approximately 20–25% between 25°C and 35°C agrees well with the temperature-dependent decrease in water viscosity over 10 °C.
source: The measured increase in mobility of sfGFP and two other constructs, by approximately 20–25% between 25°C and 35°C (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B), agrees well with the temperature-dependent decrease in water viscosity over 10 °C (Huber, 2009).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, and a citation to Huber, 2009.

claim: The growth temperature of the E. coli culture had no apparent effect on protein mobility.
source: Surprisingly, the growth temperature of the E. coli culture had no apparent effect on protein mobility (Figure 5—figure supplement 4)
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Chloramphenicol treatment caused a minor increase in cell width.
source: We observed that chloramphenicol treatment caused a minor increase in cell width (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F)
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Chloramphenicol treatment caused a decrease in cell density.
source: and a decrease in cell density (Figure 2—figure supplement 3G).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 3G.

claim: Protein mobility decreased in chloramphenicol-treated cells.
source: However, protein mobility rather decreased in chloramphenicol-treated cells, opposite to what could be expected based alone on the chloramphenicol-induced reduction of cell density (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Inhibition of RNA transcription by rifampicin treatment led to a marked increase in protein mobility.
source: In contrast, inhibition of RNA transcription by rifampicin treatment led to a marked increase in protein mobility (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The increase in protein mobility caused by rifampicin treatment was similar for all tested proteins.
source: Similar to the effects of osmolarity and temperature, the increase in protein mobility caused by the rifampicin treatment, and its decrease induced by chloramphenicol were similar for all tested proteins (Figure 5C)
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 5C.

claim: Protein mobility was significantly higher in rapidly growing cells.
source: Finally, we investigated whether protein mobility might be influenced by cell growth, comparing FCS measurements in cells incubated at 35°C on agarose pads containing either only M9 salts or M9 salts plus glucose and casamino acids. These conditions had only minor impact on the cell shape (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G, H). Although at this high-temperature residual growth was also observed for cells on M9 salt pads, cell growth in presence of nutrients was expectedly much more pronounced. The observed protein mobility was also much higher in the presence of nutrients, and this increase was again similar for the four tested differently sized constructs (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2D)
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The enhanced protein mobility in presence of nutrients appears to be primarily due to active protein production and cell growth.
source: Thus, the enhanced protein mobility in presence of nutrients appears to be primarily due to active protein production and cell growth.
evidence: This is inferred from the results of chloramphenicol treatment experiments described in the Results section and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 6.

claim: The contribution of metabolic activity to protein mobility in presence of nutrients was significant but weaker than the contribution of biosynthesis.
source: Nevertheless, even chloramphenicol-treated cells exhibited a moderate increase in protein mobility in presence of nutrients, indicating that the metabolic activity contributes to the overall effect of growth on diffusion.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 6.

claim: Lowering the energy state of the cell by DNP treatment did not reduce protein mobility for sfGFP and AcnA-sfGFP.
source: In any case, the impact of growth on diffusion of individual proteins cannot be simply explained by the energy state of the cell, since lowering it by the inhibition of respiration-dependent ATP synthesis using treatment with dinitrophenol (DNP) did not reduce protein mobility, at either 25°C or 35°C. This is contrary to the effect of the DNP treatment on large cytoplasmic particles (Parry et al., 2014; Figure 5—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 7.

claim: The mobility of Adk-sfGFP was reduced by DNP treatment at high temperature.
source: An interesting exception was the mobility of Adk-sfGFP, which was indeed reduced by the DNP treatment at high temperature.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 7.

claim: The majority of studied proteins exhibit a rather uniform relation between their molecular mass and cytoplasmic mobility, with a clear upper bound on protein mobility at a given molecular mass.
source: Here, we addressed these questions by systematically investigating the diffusive behavior of a large set of fluorescent protein fusions to differently sized cytoplasmic proteins of E. coli. We demonstrate that the majority of studied proteins exhibit a rather uniform relation between their molecular mass and cytoplasmic mobility, with a clear upper bound on protein mobility at a given molecular mass.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section and supported by Figure 1D.

claim: The apparent weak anomaly of diffusion observed in the FCS data analysis could be largely accounted for by confinement of the otherwise purely Brownian diffusing particles.
source: Furthermore, our simulations suggest that the apparent weak anomaly of diffusion observed in the FCS data analysis could be largely accounted for by confinement of the otherwise purely Brownian diffusing particles.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section and supported by Figure 2A and B.

claim: The diffusion of most proteins in the bacterial cytoplasm shows little if any deviation from Brownian within the precision of the experiments.
source: Thus, we conclude that the diffusion of most proteins in the bacterial cytoplasm shows little if any deviation from Brownian within the precision of our experiments, although some residual anomaly cannot be excluded.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section and supported by the simulation and experimental results.

claim: For small proteins, the effective viscosity of bacterial cytoplasm is only approximately six times higher than in dilute solution.
source: Given the diffusion coefficient determined in our study for free sfGFP, ~14 µm2 s–1, for small proteins this effective viscosity of bacterial cytoplasm is only approximately six times higher than in dilute solution (Potma et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section and supported by the measured diffusion coefficient for sfGFP and a citation to Potma et al., 2001.

claim: The diffusion coefficient for GFP determined in this study (~14 µm2 s–1) is substantially larger than the values reported in early FRAP studies.
source: This diffusion coefficient for GFP is substantially larger than the values reported in the early studies that used FRAP (Elowitz et al., 1999; Konopka et al., 2006; Mullineaux et al., 2006; Konopka et al., 2009; Kumar et al., 2010; Mika et al., 2010; Nenninger et al., 2010)
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section and supported by the measured diffusion coefficient for sfGFP and citations to early FRAP studies.

claim: The diffusion coefficient for GFP determined in this study is consistent with other FCS and SPT studies.
source: although it is consistent with other FCS and SPT studies (Meacci et al., 2006; English et al., 2011; Sanamrad et al., 2014; Diepold et al., 2017; Rocha et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section and supported by the measured diffusion coefficient for sfGFP and citations to other FCS and SPT studies.

claim: Differences between early FRAP and FCS/SPT measurements are apparently due to the limitations of early FRAP analyses that generally underestimated protein mobility.
source: These differences are apparently due to the limitations of early FRAP analyses that generally underestimated protein mobility, rather than due to different spatial and temporal scales assessed by the two techniques, since our direct comparison between FCS and FRAP measurements yielded similar values of diffusion coefficients.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section and supported by the comparison between FCS and FRAP measurements in Figure 3C.

claim: Protein-protein interactions may be the main cause of protein subdiffusion in bacterial cytoplasm.
source: Thus, protein-protein interactions may be the main cause of protein subdiffusion in bacterial cytoplasm, although other explanations might hold for subdiffusion of large cytoplasmic particles (Golding and Cox, 2004; Lampo et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section and supported by the results for ClpS, Map, and DnaK mutants, and citations to studies on large particles.

claim: There is apparently little organism-specific adaptation of freely diffusing proteins to their 'bacterial host,' with a possible exception of bacteria with extreme pH or ionic strength of the cytoplasm.
source: Thus, there is apparently little organism-specific adaptation of freely diffusing proteins to their 'bacterial host,' with a possible exception of bacteria with extreme pH or ionic strength of the cytoplasm (Schavemaker et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section and supported by the results for non-native proteins in Figure 4, and a citation to Schavemaker et al., 2017.

claim: The temperature dependence of the cytoplasmic viscosity in the tested range was similar to that of water and consistent with the Stokes-Einstein relation.
source: Despite multiple effects of environmental temperature on cellular processes, such as the active (nonthermal) stirring of the cytoplasm at higher temperature (Weber et al., 2012), the temperature dependence of the cytoplasmic viscosity in the tested range was similar to that of water and consistent with the Stokes-Einstein relation, decreasing by 20–30% for a temperature increase of 10°C (Huber, 2009).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section and supported by the results in Figure 5B and citations to Weber et al., 2012 and Huber, 2009.

claim: No dependence of the effective cytoplasmic viscosity on growth temperature was observed.
source: We further observed no dependence of the effective cytoplasmic viscosity on growth temperature, in contrast to the homeostatic adaptation of bacterial membrane fluidity (Sinensky, 1974) and of bacterial signaling (Oleksiuk et al., 2011; Almblad et al., 2021) to the growth temperature.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section and supported by the results in Figure 5—figure supplement 4 and citations to Sinensky, 1974, Oleksiuk et al., 2011, and Almblad et al., 2021.

claim: These perturbations to the cytoplasmic protein mobility have proportional effects on differently sized proteins.
source: Importantly, we observed that these perturbations to the cytoplasmic protein mobility, including cell growth and changes to the macromolecular crowding and temperature, have proportional effects on differently sized proteins.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section and supported by the results in Figure 5.

claim: Effects of perturbations on protein mobility can be simply accounted for by changes in the cytoplasmic viscosity.
source: These results suggest that—within the tested size range—protein diffusion in E. coli cytoplasm remains Brownian under all tested conditions, including growing cells, and effects of these perturbations on protein mobility can be simply accounted for by changes in the cytoplasmic viscosity.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section and supported by the results in Figure 5.

claim: All experiments were performed in the E. coli strain W3110.
source: All experiments were performed in the E. coli strain W3110 (Serra et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Genes of interest were cloned in frame with sfGFP into pTrc99A vector under control of the trc promoter inducible by IPTG.
source: Genes of interest were amplified by PCR using Q5 polymerase (New England Biosciences) and cloned in frame with sfGFP using Gibson assembly (Gibson et al., 2009) into pTrc99A vector (Amann et al., 1988), under control of the trc promoter inducible by isopropyl ß-D-1-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Materials and methods section.

claim: In all cases sfGFP was fused at the C-terminus of the protein of interest with a GGGGS linker.
source: In all cases sfGFP was fused at the C-terminus of the protein of interest with a GGGGS linker.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Materials and methods section.

claim: E. coli cultures were grown in M9 minimal medium supplemented with 0.2% casamino acids, 20 mM glucose, and 100 µg/ml ampicillin.
source: E. coli cultures were grown in M9 minimal medium (48 mM Na2HPO4, 22 mM KH2PO4, 8.4 mM NaCl, 18.6 mM NH4Cl, 2 mM MgSO4, and 0.1 mM CaCl2) supplemented with 0.2% casamino acids, 20 mM glucose, and 100 µg/ml ampicillin for selection.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Overnight cultures were diluted to OD600=0.035 and grown for 3.5 hr at 37°C and 200 rpm shaking.
source: The overnight cultures were diluted to OD600=0.035 and grown for 3.5 hr at 37°C and 200 rpm shaking.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Cultures were treated for additional 45 min with 100 µg/ml cephalexin and with 0–15 µM IPTG to induce expression of the fluorescent protein constructs.
source: Cultures were treated for additional 45 min, under the same temperature and shaking conditions, with 100 µg/ml cephalexin and with 0–15 µM IPTG (Table 1), to induce expression of the fluorescent protein constructs.
